source_evidence.observation: The selected result is an unnumbered, unlabelled displayed inequality introduced in running prose. It carries no theorem/lemma number, no proof, and no reference. The only stated hypotheses are (a) X is a random variable and (b) φ : R → R is convex. The conclusion is the single inequality φ(E X) ≤ E φ(X), with the expectation of X on the left inside φ and the expectation of the composite on the right. There is no second part, no equality case, and no finiteness caveat printed with it (contrast Lemma 1.2.1 two pages later, which explicitly adds "The two sides of this identity are either finite or infinite simultaneously").

MODULE DEFINABILITY POLICY (interpretation, not printed text): because the first edition defines E X as a Lebesgue integral (footnote 1) but states no exceptional-value convention for arbitrary real random variables, this module reads each ordinary real-valued E X on its finite-integral domain. For Jensen this means the configured contract carries integrability of X and integrability of φ ∘ X as premises, so that both E X and E φ(X) denote genuine real numbers and the displayed inequality is meaningful. These premises are part of the configured source contract for this module; they are not optional proof conveniences. The printed source itself states neither.
conclusions: The single inequality, printed verbatim as the centered display: "φ(E X) ≤ E φ(X)."

Direction: the value of φ at the expectation is at most (≤, non-strict) the expectation of the composite. The convex-side ordering is load-bearing; it is not stated for concave φ and not stated with the reverse or a strict inequality.
Left-hand side: φ applied to the real number E X — a function value, i.e. φ(∫_Ω X dP).
Right-hand side: E φ(X), which by footnote 2's binding convention is E[φ(X)] = E[φ ∘ X] = ∫_Ω φ(X(ω)) dP(ω) — the expectation of the transformed random variable, not a product and not (E φ)(X).
The result is single-part: there is no second clause, no equality/rigidity case, no strictness statement, no finiteness co-statement, and no converse.
definitions_and_conventions: Expectation (footnote 1, printed page 5): "the expectation E X of a random variable X on a probability space (Ω, Σ, P) is, by definition, the Lebesgue integral of the function X : Ω → R". Hence E X = ∫_Ω X dP with P a probability measure (total mass 1).

Nonlinear-binding convention (footnote 2, printed page 5): "we drop the brackets in the notation E[f (X)] and simply write E f (X) instead. Thus, nonlinear functions bind before expectation." This is what makes "E φ(X)" unambiguously E[φ ∘ X].

Convexity (footnote 3, printed page 6): "a function φ is convex if φ(λx + (1 − λ)y) ≤ λφ(x) + (1 − λ)φ(y) for all t ∈ [0, 1] and all vectors x, y in the domain of φ." Non-strict convexity; combination form; quantified over the full domain, which for φ : R → R is all of R. No continuity, differentiability, or measurability is assumed or asserted as part of this definition.
Random variable: implicitly a measurable map X : Ω → R, per footnote 1's "the function X : Ω → R". The book does not admit extended-real-valued random variables at this point.

The book states no convention for E X when X is not integrable, and no convention for arithmetic with ±∞ in the Section 1.1/1.2 material surrounding this passage. (Absence is itself part of the record; see the module definability policy in hypotheses and the ambiguities entries.)
implicit_context: Chapter framing (printed page 5, chapter opening): "In this chapter we recall some basic concepts and results of probability theory. The reader should already be familiar with most of this material" — the chapter is an unproved recall/preliminaries chapter, so this inequality is quoted without proof by design.

Section framing (printed page 6, section heading "1.2 Some classical inequalities"): Jensen is presented as the first of a list of classical inequalities (Jensen, Minkowski (1.4), Cauchy-Schwarz, Hölder), all stated in prose with displayed formulas.

The ambient probability space (Ω, Σ, P) is inherited from Section 1.1 and is never re-declared in Section 1.2; P is a probability measure, so constants are integrable and E of a constant is that constant.

The neighbouring inequalities in the same section (Minkowski, Cauchy-Schwarz, Hölder) do restrict to X, Y ∈ Lp / L2 / Lq, i.e. finite-norm classes as defined on printed page 6 ("Lp = {X : ∥X∥Lp < ∞}"). The absence of such a restriction in the Jensen sentence is therefore a per-statement choice, not a suppressed section-wide standing assumption.

ANALYST INFERENCE (not printed): for E φ(X) to be defined at all, φ ∘ X must be measurable; this holds automatically for convex φ : R → R since convexity on R forces continuity on R, but the book never says this. Flagged as inference, not source content.

details: Two universal binders, X and φ, both scoping over one conclusion; the ambient probability space is context, not a binder of the sentence.
"for any random variable X" is maximally general in the printed text — it admits non-integrable X, which the module definability policy then narrows to the finite-integral domain.

X: random variable on (Ω, Σ, P), values in R — the object whose mean is taken.
φ: deterministic real function on R — the convex transform; it is applied pointwise to X on the right-hand side and to the scalar E X on the left-hand side.
E X: a real scalar (the Lebesgue integral of X against P), used as an argument to φ.
E φ(X): a real scalar, the Lebesgue integral of the composite φ ∘ X against P.
≤ : the ordinary order on R, non-strict, between two real scalars.

The left-hand side is written "φ(E X)" with explicit parentheses around E X, so no binding ambiguity arises there.
The asymmetry of the two sides — function-then-expectation versus expectation-then-function — is the entire content of the result and must be preserved exactly.
Convexity is the book's own footnote-3 definition (non-strict combination inequality), not strict convexity and not midpoint convexity.

It is quantified over all x, y in the domain of φ, i.e. over all of R for the Jensen sentence — so this is convexity on the whole real line, not convexity on a subinterval or on the essential range of X.
The definition is stated for "vectors x, y in the domain of φ", phrasing that anticipates later vector-valued domains in the book, but at this use site the domain is R.
No regularity (continuity, measurability, differentiability, finiteness beyond R-valuedness) is stated as part of convexity here.
The source states no exceptional case: no non-integrable case, no infinite-value case, no degenerate/constant-X case, no equality case, no empty-domain case.

Contrast is instructive: Lemma 1.2.1, two pages later, explicitly adds "The two sides of this identity are either finite or infinite simultaneously". No such sentence accompanies Jensen, so the source neither asserts nor denies an extended-real reading.
Per the module definability policy, this contract fixes the finite-integral reading: Integrable X and Integrable (φ ∘ X), with both expectations real.
The selected passage is single-part; nothing is dropped by stating it as one inequality.

Display (1.3), the Lp-monotonicity ∥X∥Lp ≤ ∥X∥Lq for 0 ≤ p ≤ q ≤ ∞, is presented as "a simple consequence of Jensen's inequality" but is a distinct numbered claim outside the selected anchor and must not be folded into this contract.

contract_plain_english: In Section 1.2 of Chapter 1 (PDF page 2, printed page 6) Vershynin recalls Jensen's inequality in a single unnumbered sentence with one displayed formula: for any random variable X and any convex function φ : R → R, φ(E X) ≤ E φ(X). Three inherited conventions fix its meaning. First, footnote 1 on printed page 5 defines E X to be the Lebesgue integral of X : Ω → R over a probability space (Ω, Σ, P), so X is a real-valued random variable and expectations are integrals against a probability measure. Second, footnote 2 on the same page declares that nonlinear functions bind before expectation, so the right-hand side E φ(X) means E[φ ∘ X], the expectation of the transformed random variable — not a product and not any other parse. Third, footnote 3 on printed page 6 defines convexity in place, non-strictly, by φ(λx + (1 − λ)y) ≤ λφ(x) + (1 − λ)φ(y) over the whole domain of φ, which for φ : R → R is all of R; that footnote's quantifier is printed as "for all t ∈ [0, 1]" while the formula uses λ, an evident typographical slip. The result is single-part and universally quantified over both X and φ: no equality case, no strictness, no constants, no indices, no converse, and no finiteness co-statement of the kind that Lemma 1.2.1 carries two pages later. Crucially, the printed sentence attaches no integrability, moment, or Lp-membership hypothesis to X, even though the neighbouring Minkowski, Cauchy-Schwarz, and Hölder statements in the same section do restrict their random variables to Lp classes; and the first edition nowhere states an exceptional-value convention for E X when the Lebesgue integral fails to exist. This module's definability convention resolves that gap explicitly rather than silently: every ordinary real-valued E X is read on its finite-integral domain, so the configured contract for Jensen carries integrability of X and integrability of φ ∘ X as genuine premises that make both displayed expressions real numbers. Those premises are part of the source contract as configured for this module, not optional proof conveniences — while the record above notes plainly that they do not appear in the printed text. A faithful rendering therefore states: given a probability space, a real random variable X with X integrable and φ ∘ X integrable, and a convex φ : R → R, the real number φ(E X) is less than or equal to the real number E[φ(X)].
